questions.stem: `x^3 + x^2`. Write each term out as factors. Any factor that appears in both can be written once, out front.

work.why: Three `x`s and two `x`s. Two of them appear in both, so those two are written once; the second term is then used up and leaves 1.

aspects.body: The shared part is a count, and it is the smaller: 3 and 2 share 2. The shorter term runs out first.

questions.stem: `6x + 9`. Only one of these has an `x`, so see what is left to share.

work.why: `6x` is `2 · 3 · x` and 9 is `3 · 3`. Only the 3 appears in both; the `x` is in one term, so it stays inside.

aspects.body: A factor has to be in every term without exception. The `x` is in `6x` but not in 9, so it cannot come out.

questions.stem: `4x^2 + 10x`. The numbers split into factors too. Write out both terms, then write the shared factors once.

work.why: `4x^2` is `2 · 2 · x · x` and `10x` is `2 · 5 · x`. One 2 and one `x` appear in both.

aspects.body: Numbers split into factors the same way `x` does. 4 is `2 · 2` and 10 is `2 · 5`, so one 2 is shared and the other is not.
Write only the `x` once and you get `x(4x + 10)`. That is true, but 4 and 10 are both even, so a 2 appears in both as well.

questions.stem: `4x^2 + 4x`. Write out both terms and pull the shared factors to the front. Watch what the second term is left with.

work.why: The second term is made entirely of shared factors, so it leaves 1 rather than nothing. Without the 1 the expression would read `4x(x)`, which is `4x^2`.

aspects.body: A term used up leaves 1, not nothing. Two terms go in and two come out.

questions.stem: `6x^3 + 9x^2 + 3x`. Three terms. A factor still has to be in all of them.

work.why: All three have a 3 and one `x`. The last term is used up by them, so it leaves 1.

aspects.body: The shortest term limits everything: `3x` has only one 3 and one `x`, so that is all any of them can share.

questions.stem: `-6x - 15`. Both terms are negative, so the minus can come out with the rest.

work.why: Taking the minus out with the 3 leaves both terms inside positive: `−3 × 2x` is `-6x`, and `−3 × 5` is `-15`.

aspects.body: Write only 3 out front and the bracket keeps its minus signs: `3(-2x - 5)`. Both are correct. Taking the minus out as well leaves every term inside the bracket positive.
This is the second pair of `4x^2 + 10x - 6x - 15`, and its bracket comes out as `2x + 5` — the same bracket the first pair gave.

questions.stem: `2x(2x+5) - 3(2x+5)`. These are the two pieces you just factored, added together. What both terms have now is a whole bracket.

work.why: `2x+5` appears in both terms, so it is written once in front, exactly as a number or an `x` would be.

aspects.body: A bracket is a factor like any other. Nothing about writing it once is different; only what the terms share has changed.
This is the second half of factoring by grouping, and grouping is how `2x^2 + 7x + 3` is factored once the middle term is split.
